title: Who protects the antivirus? How we secure Malwarebytes itself
content_md: An antivirus is also software, and it can have weaknesses of its own. That makes antivirus development particularly demanding. The product must safely handle files that may be hostile, run reliably across very different Windows environments, and resist attackers who try to abuse its privileges or shut it down completely. Imagine a piece of malware that can disable your antivirus and leave you unprotected. That’s exactly what we as engineers work to prevent. The attack surface of a privileged process You might wonder why vulnerabilities matter for a desktop application that runs locally. Our software runs with high privileges, so it has access to the entire system. That access is what lets it protect the system from exploits, data theft, and ransomware. It also makes our software an attractive target. An attacker who can disable our protection, or abuse it to gain those privileges, has a much easier path to taking over the system. Two layers, one critical boundary At a basic level, Malwarebytes has two layers: a user interface running as the signed-in user, and a background service running as SYSTEM. They communicate through COM (Component Object Model), a built-in Windows mechanism that lets one program call functions in another program, even one running in a separate process. The UI can’t do much on its own. When you add an exclusion, restore a file from quarantine, or pause real-time protection, the UI only asks, and the SYSTEM service does the work.
